blocks.text: The Mental Model That Explains Everything
Most Git confusion disappears once you understand that your changes move between three places. Nearly every command either moves content between these areas or inspects the difference between them.

git checkout / git switch / git restore
A proposed snapshot of the next commit, stored in the binary file .git/index
The object database and refs inside .git: all commits ever made

blocks.text:
$ echo "print('hello')" > app.py
$ git status --short
?? app.py            # untracked: Git has never seen this file

$ git add app.py
$ git status --short
A  app.py            # staged: will be in the next commit

$ git commit -m "Add hello script"
[main (root-commit) 3f2a1c9] Add hello script
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

$ git status --short
                     # clean: working tree == index == HEAD

items: Untracked: exists in the working tree but not in the index or the last commit.
Unmodified: tracked, and identical in working tree, index and HEAD.
Modified: working tree differs from the index.
Staged: index differs from HEAD, so the change will be part of the next commit.

blocks.text: The Index Is a Snapshot, Not a Checklist

A common misunderstanding is that git add marks a file to be committed. It does more than that: it copies the file's content, as it is at that moment, into the index. If you edit the file again afterwards, the index still holds the old version. A single file can therefore be both staged and modified at the same time.

$ echo "v1" > notes.txt && git add notes.txt
$ echo "v2" >> notes.txt
$ git status --short
AM notes.txt         # A = added to index, M = modified again since

$ git diff --staged  # shows only 'v1' (what will be committed)
$ git diff           # shows the extra 'v2' line (not yet staged)
If you commit now, only "v1" is committed. Always run git status before committing, and re-run git add after further edits.

items: Crafting focused commits: you changed five files but only three belong to this logical change. Stage those three.
Partial staging: git add -p lets you stage individual hunks of a file, splitting unrelated edits in the same file into separate commits.
Review checkpoint: git diff --staged shows exactly what you are about to record.
Merge conflict resolution: during a conflicted merge, the index holds multiple versions (stages 1, 2 and 3) of conflicting files. Marking a conflict resolved is literally git add.

blocks.text: git commit -a stages all modifications and deletions of tracked files, then commits. It skips untracked files entirely, so a newly created file is silently left out. It is convenient, but it removes the review step the index exists for.
